title: The examination of conscience
hookLine: a slow look back using the commandments or the beatitudes

cards: Eleven at night, lights off, and the day starts replaying. That thing you said at lunch. The email you sent too fast.
The tape runs again and again, and it isn't kind.

Catholics keep an old practice that does the same review on purpose, slowly, with a guide, and in a different voice: not a prosecutor, more like a good doctor, honest about what's wrong and on your side.
This week i'll follow it all the way into the confessional. It starts with one word: conscience.

teach.b: Conscience comes from Latin, conscientia: knowing with. Knowing something together with yourself, the part of you that sees what you did and knows what it meant.

The Catholic Church teaches that conscience is where a person is alone with God, a kind of inner sanctuary where God's voice can be heard, and that everyone is bound to follow a well-formed conscience.

John Henry Newman, the English convert and cardinal, put it memorably in 1875: "Conscience is the aboriginal Vicar of Christ." Aboriginal means first, original: before any pope or priest, there's that voice within.
An examination of conscience is the practice of listening to it on purpose. Before confession, Catholics often go slowly through a guide.
A common one uses the Ten Commandments: have I put anything in God's place? Have I been honest? Have I treated my parents with respect?
Another uses the Beatitudes: have I been merciful? Have I made peace, or stirred things up? Some use the works of mercy.
Some do a short version every night.
An examination is not a trial where you're the defendant. Catholic spiritual writers warn against scrupulosity, a harsh, anxious picking at yourself that never finds rest.
The point of looking is to see clearly enough to be healed.
You look honestly, because you can't ask forgiveness for what you won't admit. And you look without harshness, because the one you're looking with, Catholics believe, is merciful.
Tomorrow, through the door of the confessional.

how: Before confession, and often each night, Catholics examine their conscience with a printed guide based on the Ten Commandments, the Beatitudes or the works of mercy.

the inner voice where Catholics believe you meet God

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: an examination of conscience is meant to feel like a trial
spiritual writers warn against harshness and scruples; the point is to see clearly and be healed.
Catholics may use the Beatitudes to examine their conscience
the commandments, the Beatitudes and the works of mercy are all common guides.

games.q: you're lying awake replaying something you said today. what does an examination of conscience ask you to do?
o: keep replaying it until you feel bad enough.
name it plainly, and look at it with mercy.
push it away and think about something else.
games.why: honestly, not harshly: name it clearly enough to ask forgiveness, without the anxious picking the tradition calls scrupulosity.

practice: Go back through the last day like a film, from waking up until now: where were you patient, where were you short with someone, where were you honest, where did you shade the truth?
Notice without judging, name anything that stands out plainly, then name one thing you did well, because that belongs in the look back too. If you pray, hand both to God.

wordCard.voice: Conscience. From the Latin for knowing with. The inner voice Catholics believe is where a person meets God, and a slow, honest look back by its light. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: knowing with, knowing together; con-, with, and scientia, knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: look honestly, not harshly. More like a good doctor than a prosecutor. Rest easy.
